The 1st respondent in Op(Mv).1339/2002 on the file of the Motor
Accidents Claims Tribunal, Attingal, is the appellant.

The above Op was filed under Section 163A of
the Motor V
ehicles Act claiming compensation for the injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident that occurred on 25.7.2002.(The

parties are hereafter referred to as per their rank before the Tribunal.).
2.

The above OP was filed by the mother, sister and the minor children of the predeceased brother of the deceased, who are dependents of the deceased Krishnankutty Nair, who died in a motor vehicle accident that occurred on 25.7.2002.

According to the petitioners on 25.7.2002 at about 12.30 pm while the deceased was reversing the lorry bearing registration No.KL01/D6597 along the Kalladichavila -Charumoodu, for giving way to another lorry, it capsized by land sliding to a depth of R.Vijayan (Deceased)* vs S.Jayanthakumari on 12 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67534141/
2 about 25 metres.
In the accident, he sustained serious injuries and he succumbed to the injuries on the same day.
Respondents 1 and 2 are the registered owner and injurer of the lorry involved in the accident.
3. The 2nd respondent, the insurer who alone contested the case before the Tribunal filed written statements alleging negligence on the part of the 2025:KER:21529 deceased himself.

It was also contended that the said lorry had no fitness certificate and hence they denied having any liability to indemnify the compensation, if any awarded against the 1st respondent.
4.
The evidence in the case consists of Exts.A1 to A12 and B1.
After evaluating the evidence on record, the Tribunal awarded a compensation of Rs.3,44,500/- and directed the 1st respondent to pay the same.
The Tribunal exonerated the 2nd respondent on the ground that there was no fitness certificate to the lorry, at the time of the accident.
Being aggrieved by the above order of the Tribunal, mulcting the liability on him, the 1 st respondent preferred this Appeal.

During the pendency of the appeal, the 1 st respondent/appellant died and his legal representatives were impleaded as additional appellants 2 and 3.
5.
Now the point that arise for consideration is the following :

Whether the finding of the Tribunal exonerating the 2 nd respondent from indemnifying the compensation due to the petitioners from the 1 st respondent, is liable to be interfered with, in the light of the grounds raised in the appeal ?
6. In this case the accident as well as the death of the deceased in the accident are not in dispute.
The 2nd respondent would also admit that there was valid policy to the offending lorry.

However,
their contention is that on the date of the accident on 25.7.2002, the lorry did not have valid fitness certificate and 2025
as such, they are not liable to indemnify the compensation awarded by the Tribunal against the 1st respondent.
The Tribunal accepted the above argument of the 2nd respondent and mulcted the 1st respondent with the liability to pay the compensation to the petitioners.
7. During the pendency of the appeal before this court also the 1 st respondent could not dispute the fact that the offending lorry had no valid fitness certificate at the time of the accident.

On the other hand, the learned counsel for the 1st respondent would argue that in the absence of any evidence to prove that the accident occurred due to any mechanical defects, the absence of fitness certificate is not sufficient to exonerate the insurer.

On the other hand, the learned counsel for the 2nd respondent relying upon the decision of this Court in Pareed Pillai v. Oriental Insurance Co.Ltd,
2018 (5) KHC 1, would argue that absence of fitness certificate to transport vehicle is a fundamental breach of the policy conditions and as such, the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the insurer.

sentences.text: the case of a transport vehicle and one requirement cannot be segregated from the other

. The transport vehicle should be completely fit and road worthy, to be plied on the road, which otherwise may cause threat to the lives and limbs of passengers and the general public, apart from damage to property.

Only if the transport vehicle is having valid Fitness Certificate, would the necessary permit be issued in terms of Section 66 of the Act and by virtue of the mandate under Section 56 of the Act, no transport vehicle without Fitness Certificate will be deemed as a validly registered vehicle for the purpose of Section 39 of the Act,
which stipulates that nobody shall drive or cause the motor vehicle to be driven without valid registration in public place or such other place, as the case may be.

These requirements are quite 'fundamental' in MACA No. 2030 of 2015 and connected cases nature; unlike a case where a transport vehicle carrying more passengers than the permitted capacity or a goods carriage carrying excess quantity of goods than the permitted extent or a case where a transport vehicle was plying through a deviated route than the one shown in the route permit which instances could rather be branded as 'technical violations'.

In other words, when a transport vehicle is not having a Fitness Certificate, it will be deemed as having no Certificate of Registration and when such vehicle is not having Permit or Fitness Certificate,
nobody can drive such vehicle and no owner can permit the use of any such vehicle compromising with the lives, limbs, properties of the passengers/general public.

Obviously, since the safety of passengers and general public was of serious concern and consideration for the law makers, appropriate and adequate measures were taken by incorporating relevant provisions in the Statute, also pointing out the circumstances which would constitute offence; providing adequate penalty.

This being the position, such lapse, if any, can only be regarded as a fundamental breach and not a technical breach and any interpretation to the contrary, will only negate the intention of the law makers.

2025:KER:21529 8. In the decision in Oriental Insurance Co.Ltd. v. Abdul Salam and Ors., MANU/KE/3494/2020,
Prasannamma v. Chandran and Ors., MANU/KE/0853/2022, United India Insurance Co.Ltd., v.
Geo C.A. and Ors., 2022 (6) KHC 162 and Ahammed Abdulla v. The New India Assurance Co.LTd.,
and Ors., MANU/KE/0201/2023, this Court following the decision in Pareed Pillai (supra) held that absence of fitness certificate is a fundamental breach and as such, the insurer is entitled to get an order of pay and recovery from the owner.

In the above circumstances, the deceased being the employee of the 1st respondent can claim only the compensation due to him under the proviso (c) to Section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act.

10. Section 4 of the Employees Compensation Act reads as follows :-

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the amount of compensation shall be as follows, namely:
(a) where death results from the injury an amount equal to fifty per cent of the monthly wages of the deceased employee multiplied by the relevant factor; or an amount of one lakh and twenty thousand rupees, whichever is more."
11.

Since the monthly income of the deceased claimed in the petition is Rs.3000/-, as per Section 4 of the Employees Compensation Act, the 2025:KER:21529 compensation payable is an amount equal to 50% of the monthly wages of the deceased employee multiplied by the relevant factor; or an amount of one lakh and twenty thousand rupees, whichever is more.
12. Since he was aged 40, the factor applicable is 184.17.
Therefore, the compensation payable will come to Rs.2,76,255/- (50% of Rs.3000/- x 184.17).
13. However, in this case, the Tribunal has awarded a compensation of Rs.3,43,500/- which is more than what is due under the proviso (c) to Section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act.
Therefore, in the absence of any appeal by the respondents, this Appeal is liable to be dismissed, confirming the Award passed by the Tribunal.
In the result, this Appeal is dismissed.
Considering the facts, I order no costs.
